description: Composite group containing panels (b), (c) and (d) of Fig. 3 (panel (a) is not present in the supplied images). (b) Engineering stress-strain curves: x-axis "Engineering Strain/%" 0-50 (ticks every 10), y-axis "Engineering Stress/MPa" 0-1200 (ticks every 200), with three colour-coded curves labelled 0Cr (black), 3Cr (red) and 6Cr (blue). The 0Cr curve reaches the highest stress at the lowest strain but flattens into a plateau, shows a small peak near ~950 MPa and then fractures first, at about 28% strain; the 3Cr and 6Cr curves rise continuously to beyond 30% strain, ending above the 1000 MPa gridline with 6Cr extending furthest. (c) and (d) are dual-axis plots combining true stress-strain curves (solid) and strain hardening rate curves (dashed) of the as-cast (c) and annealed (d) strips; left axis "True Stress(MPa)" 0-1600 (tick 200), right axis "Strain Hardening Rate (dσ/dε) MPa" 0-4000 (tick 500), x-axis "True Strain" 0.00-0.40 (tick 0.05). Curves are labelled 0Cr, 3Cr, 6Cr with arrows, and two horizontal green dotted guide lines cross each panel. In (c) the 0Cr hardening-rate curve shows a distinct hump whereas the 3Cr and 6Cr dashed curves decay monotonically from high initial values; in (d) the dashed hardening-rate curves lie overall lower, with a near-plateau for 3Cr. Solid true-stress curves approach 1400 MPa at the largest strains.

observations.observation: Panel (b) shows engineering stress-strain curves with axes 'Engineering Strain/%' (0-50, tick 10) and 'Engineering Stress/MPa' (0-1200, tick 200) and three colour-coded, text-labelled curves: 0Cr (black), 3Cr (red) and 6Cr (blue).

In (b) the 0Cr curve is the first to reach its plateau and the first to fail (sharp drop at roughly 28% strain, below the 1000 MPa gridline), whereas the 3Cr and 6Cr curves continue to rise until roughly 33-36% strain and terminate above the 1000 MPa gridline, with 6Cr extending furthest in strain.

Panels (c) and (d) are dual-axis plots: left axis 'True Stress(MPa)' 0-1600 (tick 200), right axis 'Strain Hardening Rate (dσ/dε) MPa' 0-4000 (tick 500), x-axis 'True Strain' 0.00-0.40 (tick 0.05); solid curves are true stress and dashed curves are strain hardening rate.

Two horizontal green dotted guide lines run across panel (c) and across panel (d), lying at roughly the 1500-1600 MPa and 2000-2200 MPa levels of the right (strain-hardening-rate) axis; they sit lower on the right axis in (d) than in (c).

In (c) the dashed strain hardening rate curve of the Cr-free strip (0Cr) exhibits a pronounced hump, while the dashed curves of the Cr-containing strips decrease monotonically from their high initial values.

In (d) the dashed strain hardening rate curves lie at overall lower levels than the corresponding curves in (c); the 3Cr (red) dashed curve is nearly flat over a broad strain interval (a plateau), and the 6Cr (blue) dashed curve remains high for much of the strain range before falling steeply.

In (c) and (d) the solid true-stress curves increase monotonically with true strain and approach about 1400 MPa (near the 1400 MPa gridline) at their largest strains, with small vertical drops at the end of the 3Cr and 6Cr curves indicating fracture.

The figure group supplied contains only panels (b), (c) and (d); the engineering stress-strain curves of the as-cast strips (panel (a)) referenced by the caption are not present in the supplied image.

The caption states that (b) is the engineering stress-strain curve of the annealed steel strip and that (c) and (d) are the true stress-strain and strain hardening rate curves of the as-cast (c) and annealed (d) steel strips.
The citing text states that annealing increases the yield strength of the 0Cr, 3Cr and 6Cr steel strips by 131 MPa, 277 MPa and 141 MPa, respectively.

The citing text states that the addition of Cr significantly decreases the yield strength but has no obvious effect on the elongation of the Fe-20Mn-9Al-1.2C steel strip, and that the highest product UTS × TE (38.0 GPa %) is achieved in the as-cast 6Cr steel strip.

The citing text states that the strain hardening rate of all annealed steel strips is lower than that of the corresponding as-cast strips, that the annealed Cr-free strip shows a double hump of higher amplitude, that the annealed 3Cr strip shows a nearly stable platform, and that the annealed 6Cr strip decreases monotonically.

The citing text attributes the double hump in the strain hardening rate of the annealed 0Cr strip to slip-band refinement (first hump) and microband formation (second hump), and links the weaker hump of the Cr-containing strips to a smaller number of nano-scale κ-carbides.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress-strain curves of the annealed steel strips, Engineering Strain/% 0-50 vs Engineering Stress/MPa 0-1200. Three curves labelled 0Cr (black), 3Cr (red), 6Cr (blue). 0Cr reaches the highest plateau stress at lowest strain and fractures earliest (~28% strain); 3Cr and 6Cr rise gradually past 1000 MPa to ~33-36% strain, with 6Cr extending furthest.

Dual-axis plot for the as-cast strips: solid true stress-strain curves (left axis, True Stress 0-1600 MPa) and dashed strain hardening rate curves (right axis, dσ/dε 0-4000 MPa) vs True Strain 0.00-0.40, colour-coded 0Cr/3Cr/6Cr with arrow labels and two horizontal green dotted guide lines. The 0Cr dashed curve shows a pronounced hump; 3Cr and 6Cr dashed curves decrease monotonically from high initial values.

Dual-axis plot for the annealed strips in the same format as (c). Dashed strain hardening rate curves lie at lower levels than in (c); the 3Cr (red) dashed curve forms a broad near-plateau, the 6Cr (blue) dashed curve stays high over much of the strain range before falling, and the 0Cr (black) dashed curve shows a lower, multi-featured profile. Solid true-stress curves end near 1400 MPa at the largest strains.
